scenes.heading: Slices: Length, Capacity & append
scenes.narration: Let's unpack Slices: Length, Capacity, and append, the three ideas that explain almost every slice surprise in Go.

scenes.heading: The slice header
items: A slice is three words: pointer, length, capacity
Length is how many elements you can index
Capacity is room before a reallocation
Copying a slice copies the header, not the data
scenes.narration: A slice is not the data itself; it is a small three-word header. It holds a pointer to a backing array, a length that says how many elements you can index and range over, and a capacity that says how many fit before append must allocate a bigger array. Because it's just a header, copying a slice copies those three words, so two slices can share the same backing data.

scenes.heading: How append grows
steps: If room exists, write in place
If not, allocate a larger array
scenes.narration: When you append, Go first checks for spare capacity. If there's room, it writes into the existing array in place and returns a slice with a larger length. If capacity is exhausted, it allocates a new, larger array, often about double the size, copies the existing elements across, and returns a header pointing at that new array. That's exactly why you must always assign the result back with s equals append.

scenes.heading: Watch len and cap change
scenes.narration: Run this and you can watch the header evolve. We start with length zero and capacity two. Length grows by one on every append, but capacity jumps in steps: from two, to four, to eight, each time append overflows and reallocates. Notice that we assign the result of append back to s every time. Forget that assignment and your slice silently stays empty.

scenes.text: Slicing shares the backing array, so s[i:j] can alias and silently mutate the original.
scenes.narration: Here's the classic trap. Slicing with s of i to j does not copy anything; it creates a new header over the same backing array. So writing through the sub-slice can change the original, until an append forces a reallocation. When you need truly independent data, use copy into a fresh slice.
